derivations.claim: [The quotient is a complex vector space] Since $\mathbb C$ is commutative, for each $c\in\mathbb C$ the $\mathbb Z$-linear self-map $L_c$ of $F$ induced by $e_{(u,v)}\mapsto e_{(cu,v)}$ maps every defining generator of $H_0$ to a defining generator: $L_c(e_{(u+u',v)}-e_{(u,v)}-e_{(u',v)})=e_{(cu+cu',v)}-e_{(cu,v)}-e_{(cu',v)}$ is the first relation at $(cu,cu',v)$, the second family is preserved in the same way, and $L_c(e_{(ur,v)}-e_{(u,rv)})=e_{(c(ur),v)}-e_{(cu,rv)}$ is the third relation at $(cu,r,v)$ because $c(ur)=(cu)r$. Hence $L_c[H_0]\subseteq H_0$ and $L_c$ descends to a $\mathbb Z$-linear map of $F/H_0$; because $L_cL_{c'}=L_{cc'}$ and the actions distribute over the abelian group, $F/H_0$ becomes a $\mathbb C$-vector space with $c\cdot(u\otimes v)=(cu)\otimes v$; the third relation gives $(cu)\otimes v=u\otimes(cv)$, so the quotient is the $\mathbb C$-bilinear tensor product $H\odot K$. [given, F1, algebra]

[Well-definedness and sesquilinearity] For fixed $(u_0,v_0)$ the map $(u,v)\mapsto\langle u,u_0\rangle_H\langle v,v_0\rangle_K$ is $\mathbb C$-linear on $H\times K$ (both factors are linear in their first argument by [F3]) and vanishes on each generating relation of $H_0$: for the additive relations by bilinearity of the pairings, and for $(ur,v)-(u,rv)$ because $\langle ur,u_0\rangle\langle v,v_0\rangle=\langle u,u_0\rangle\langle rv,v_0\rangle$ holds in the commutative field $\mathbb C$ with the $\mathbb C$-module structures. Hence it descends to a $\mathbb C$-linear functional of the first tensor argument, and the two-variable form descends in its first argument; interchanging the roles and using conjugate symmetry of both pairings gives that it also descends in the second argument and is conjugate-linear there. Finally $\langle z,w\rangle=\overline{\langle w,z\rangle}$ because both factor pairings have this property and complex conjugation is multiplicative. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

[Positive definiteness and unique orthonormal coordinates] Let $z=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\otimes v_i$, let $U_0=\operatorname{span}\{u_i\}$ and $V_0=\operatorname{span}\{v_i\}$, and choose orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ of $U_0$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$ of $V_0$ by [F4]. Write $u_i=\sum_a\alpha_{ia}e_a$ and $v_i=\sum_b\beta_{ib}f_b$; bilinearity of $\otimes$ (step 1.1) gives $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}e_a\otimes f_b$ with $c_{ab}=\sum_i\alpha_{ia}\beta_{ib}$. By the defining formula of the Statement and orthonormality, $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b,c,d}c_{ab}\overline{c_{cd}}\langle e_a,e_c\rangle\langle f_b,f_d\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2\ge0$. If $z=0$, then this same displayed formula gives $\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2=\langle z,z\rangle=0$, so every $c_{ab}=0$, because a sum of nonnegative real numbers vanishes only if every term does; conversely, if $c_{ab}=0$ for all $a,b$ then bilinearity gives $z=\sum_{a,b}0\cdot e_a\otimes f_b=0$. Hence $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly when $z=0$, and applying the same argument to the difference of two expansions shows that the coefficients relative to orthonormal families are unique. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4, F6, algebra]

[Completion and the norm of elementary tensors] By steps 1.2 and 2.1, $(H\odot K,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a complex inner product space with induced norm $\|z\|=\langle z,z\rangle^{1/2}$ by [F3]. Its norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ exists by [F2], and by [F2] it carries a unique inner product extending the given one whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is a Hilbert space and $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image. The norm of an elementary tensor is $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|^2=\langle u\otimes v,u\otimes v\rangle=\langle u,u\rangle_H\langle v,v\rangle_K=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2$, hence $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$. Uniqueness up to isometry fixing $H\odot K$ is the uniqueness assertion of the completion construction. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

[Orthonormal family of products] Let $(e_a)_{a\in A}$, $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ be orthonormal with closed linear spans $H$ and $K$. For pairs $(a,b)\ne(a',b')$ at least one index differs, so $\langle\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b),\kappa(e_{a'}\otimes f_{b'})\rangle=\langle e_a,e_{a'}\rangle_H\langle f_b,f_{b'}\rangle_K=0$, and for equal pairs the value is $1$; hence the products are orthonormal in $\widehat{H\odot K}$. [step 3.1, F1, algebra]

[Density of the product span] Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\otimes v_i\in H\odot K$. By [F5] applied to $(e_a)$ and to $(f_b)$ there are finite sets $A_i\subseteq A$, $B_i\subseteq B$ with $\|u_i-\sum_{a\in A_i}\langle u_i,e_a\rangle e_a\|<\varepsilon/(n(\|v_i\|+1))$ and $\|v_i-\sum_{b\in B_i}\langle v_i,f_b\rangle f_b\|<\varepsilon/(n(\|u_i\|+1))$; write $u_i',v_i'$ for the finite sums and $z'=\sum_i u_i'\otimes v_i'$. Then $z-z'=\sum_i\bigl((u_i-u_i')\otimes v_i+u_i'\otimes(v_i-v_i')\bigr)$, and by the triangle inequality, $\|u_i'\|\le\|u_i\|$ (Bessel, [F5]) and the norm formula of step 3.1, $\|z-z'\|\le\sum_i\bigl(\|u_i-u_i'\|\,\|v_i\|+\|u_i\|\,\|v_i-v_i'\|\bigr)<2\varepsilon$. Hence every element of the dense subspace $\kappa[H\odot K]$ is approximated by finite sums $\sum c_{ab}\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b)$, so the closed linear span of the product family contains $\kappa[H\odot K]$ and therefore coincides with $\widehat{H\odot K}$; by [F5] the family is a complete orthonormal system. If $A$ and $B$ are countable, then $A\times B$ is countable and the closed span of a countable family is separable, so $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F5, F6, algebra] ∎

derivations.claim: [Boundedness, norm and linearity] $T_{u,v}$ is linear and $\|T_{u,v}x\|=|\langle x,v\rangle|\,\|u\|\le\|x\|\,\|v\|\,\|u\|$ by [F4], so $\|T_{u,v}\|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$ [F6]; if $u\ne0$ and $v\ne0$, taking $x=v/\|v\|$ gives $T_{u,v}x=\|v\|u$ and hence $\|T_{u,v}\|\ge\|u\|\,\|v\|$, while for $u=0$ or $v=0$ the operator vanishes and both sides are $0$. Linearity in $u$ and conjugate-linearity in $v$ are immediate from the definition and the pairing conventions [F4]. [given, F4, F6, algebra]

[Trace class and trace norm] The range of $T_{u,v}$ is contained in $\mathbb Cu$, so $T_{u,v}$ has rank at most one, is finite rank, compact, and trace class [F1]; its one-term nuclear representation is $T_{u,v}=\sum_jT_{v_j,u_j}$ with $v_1=u$, $u_1=v$ and the remaining terms zero, so $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|=\|v\|\,\|u\|$ and [F2] gives $\|T_{u,v}\|_1\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$, while $\|T_{u,v}\|_1\ge\|T_{u,v}\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$ by [F1] and step 1.1. Hence $\|T_{u,v}\|_1=\|u\|\,\|v\|$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

[The trace] Applying [F3] to the one-term nuclear representation of step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$. In particular $\operatorname{tr}(T_{x,x})=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2$ and, with step 2.1, $\|T_{x,x}\|_1=\|x\|^2$. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

[Adjoint, positivity and one-sided products] For all $x,y$, $\langle T_{u,v}x,y\rangle=\langle x,v\rangle\langle u,y\rangle=\langle x,\langle y,u\rangle v\rangle$ by [F4], so $T_{u,v}^*=T_{v,u}$; also $\langle T_{x,x}y,y\rangle=|\langle y,x\rangle|^2\ge0$, so $T_{x,x}\ge0$ by [F6]. For bounded $B$: $(BT_{u,v})x=B(\langle x,v\rangle u)=\langle x,v\rangle Bu=T_{Bu,v}x$ and $(T_{u,v}B)x=\langle Bx,v\rangle u=\langle x,B^*v\rangle u=T_{u,B^*v}x$, using the defining property of the adjoint [F4]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F6, algebra]

[Trace-norm continuity] By the bilinearity of step 1.1, $T_{u,v}-T_{u',v'}=T_{u-u',v}+T_{u',v-v'}$; by [F5] and the estimates of steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\|T_{u,v}-T_{u',v'}\|_1\le\|u-u'\|\,\|v\|+\|u'\|\,\|v-v'\|$, which tends to $0$ whenever $(u',v')\to(u,v)$ in $H\times H$; hence $(u,v)\mapsto T_{u,v}$ is continuous into $\mathcal S_1(H)$, and fixing one slot gives the stated continuity. This is (f). [step 1.1, step 2.1, F5, algebra]

This is well defined and $\mathbb C$-linear on $H\odot K$ because $(u,v)\mapsto Su\otimes Tv$ is $\mathbb C$-bilinear, composition of the linear maps $S,T$ with the bilinear tensor map; thus $R_0$ is the unique linear map on $H\odot K$ with $R_0(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$. [given, F1, algebra]

[One-sided norm estimates] Let $z=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\otimes v_i\in H\odot K$. Let $V_0=\operatorname{span}\{v_i\}$ and let $f_1,\dots,f_q$ be an orthonormal basis of $V_0$; grouping the expansion of each $v_i$ in this basis gives $z=\sum_{b=1}^q u_b\otimes f_b$ with $u_b\in\operatorname{span}\{u_i\}$. By the norm formula of [F1] and $\|Su_b\|\le\|S\|\,\|u_b\|$, $\|(S\otimes I)z\|^2=\sum_{b}\|Su_b\|^2\le\|S\|^2\sum_b\|u_b\|^2=\|S\|^2\|z\|^2$, so the map $S\otimes I_K$ on elementary tensors is bounded with norm at most $\|S\|$; symmetrically $\|(I_H\otimes T)z\|\le\|T\|\,\|z\|$. Hence $\|R_0z\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|\,\|z\|$ for all $z\in H\odot K$, because $R_0$ is the composite of the two one-sided maps on elementary tensors and the estimates compose. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

[Extension to the completions] By [F2] applied to the dense subspace $H\odot K$ of $H\widehat\otimes K$ and the Banach space $H'\widehat\otimes K'$, the map $R_0$ has a unique bounded linear extension $S\otimes T:H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ of the same norm; by step 2.1 its norm is at most $\|S\|\,\|T\|$, and uniqueness also shows that $(S\otimes T)\kappa=\kappa'\circ R_0$. This is clause (a). [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2]

[Products and commutation] For $u\otimes v$ one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')(u\otimes v)=\kappa''(SS'u\otimes TT'v)=(SS'\otimes TT')(u\otimes v)$; the two maps are bounded and agree on the dense subspace $H\odot K$, hence everywhere by uniqueness of bounded extensions, giving the first identity of (b). Taking $T'=I_K$, $S'=I_H$ and using $I\otimes I=I$ shows $(S\otimes I_K)(I_H\otimes T)=S\otimes T$; applying the same identity with the roles exchanged gives $(I_H\otimes T)(S\otimes I_K)=S\otimes T$, since $SI_H=S$ and $I_K T=T$. derivations.claim: [Expansion of a density operator] Let $\rho$ be a density operator. By [F4] and [F1] it is compact, self-adjoint and positive, so [F3] applies: its positive eigenvalues $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ have finite multiplicities, accumulate only at $0$, and $\rho x=\sum_k\mu_kP_kx$ with $P_k$ the orthogonal projection onto $E_{\mu_k}(\rho)$. Each $E_{\mu_k}(\rho)$ is finite-dimensional, so it has an orthonormal basis by [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]; listing the vectors of all these bases in one sequence $(u_n)$ with the corresponding eigenvalues $w_n>0$ enumerated by [F3] (the multiset is finite or countably infinite) gives an orthonormal family with $\rho x=\sum_nw_n\langle x,u_n\rangle u_n$, that is, $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ in operator norm, and [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=\|\rho\|_1=1$. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

[Weighted sums are density operators] Conversely let $(u_n)$ be orthonormal and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$. The series $\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ is nuclear with $\sum_nw_n\|u_n\|\,\|u_n\|=\sum_nw_n<\infty$, so it converges in operator norm to a trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\|\rho\|_1\le\sum_nw_n=1$ by [F1]; it is self-adjoint, and $\langle\rho x,x\rangle=\sum_nw_n|\langle x,u_n\rangle|^2\ge0$ by continuity of the pairing and nonnegativity of each term, so $\rho$ is positive; [F1] and [F2] give $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n\langle u_n,u_n\rangle=\sum_nw_n=1$ by linearity and absolute convergence. Hence $\rho$ is a density operator. Distinct orthonormal bases of a single positive eigenspace produce different families $(u_n)$ with the same sum, so expansions are not unique. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

[The scalar law of a PVM] Let $E$ be a PVM on $(X,\Sigma)$ and let $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ be an expansion from step 1.1 (any expansion gives the same value below by step 1.2 and [F2]). For $B\in\Sigma$, $T_{u_n,u_n}E(B)=T_{E(B)u_n,u_n}$, so by linearity of the trace and trace-norm convergence of the series (traced against the bounded $E(B)$), $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))=\sum_nw_n\operatorname{tr}(T_{E(B)u_n,u_n})=\sum_nw_n\langle E(B)u_n,u_n\rangle=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$, the series converging absolutely with value in $[0,1]$ because the finite subsums are bounded by $\sum w_n\|u_n\|^2=1$ by [F5]. Setting $B=X$ gives $\mu_\rho(X)=\sum_nw_n=1$. If $B_k$ are pairwise disjoint with union $B$, then for each $n$ the identity $\|E(B)u_n\|^2=\sum_k\|E(B_k)u_n\|^2$ holds by strong additivity of $E$ and continuity of the norm ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]); summing the resulting absolutely convergent nonnegative double series by [F7] gives $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_k\mu_\rho(B_k)$. Thus $\mu_\rho$ is a probability measure; for $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$ step 1.2 applies with $w_1=1$, giving $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, F5, F7, algebra]

[Moments for a self-adjoint operator, under AC] Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $\psi\in D(A)$ with $\|\psi\|=1$ and $E_A$ the PVM of $A$. By [F6], $A\psi=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)\psi$ and $\int\lambda^2dE_{A,\psi}=\|\Phi_{E_A}(\lambda)\psi\|^2=\|A\psi\|^2$. Since $\psi\in D(A)$ the integral $\int|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite, because $|\lambda|\le(1+\lambda^2)/2$ and $\int dE_{A,\psi}=1$; the truncations $\lambda_n:=\lambda\mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}$ satisfy $|\lambda_n|\le|\lambda|$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda$ pointwise, so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] applied to the finite measures $E_{A,\psi}$ gives $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}=\lim_n\int\lambda_n\,dE_{A,\psi}$. Finally [F6] applied to $f=|\lambda|^{1/2}$ gives $\int|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and in that case the mean integral is finite. [given, F6, algebra] ∎
